The short answer is no—you can’t tell from a single description whether this means you have clinical depression. Anxiety triggers real physical symptoms including tightness or sharp sensations in the chest wall, but having those doesn’t automatically mean you meet the criteria for Major Depressive Disorder (or even persistent depressive disorder). The Jessica Lange quote [Source: Web: Jessica Lange] shows someone describing how she’s lived with bouts of depression over time, but her personal testimony about sadness fueling creativity isn’t diagnostic evidence linking anxiety-induced pain to specific mental health diagnoses.

What we do know from general medical knowledge—and what aligns loosely with the Thorax article noting that not all chest pain involves heart conditions—is that many non-cardiac factors cause this sensation. Upper respiratory infections and shingles can produce rib/chest discomfort before other symptoms appear; activity-related muscle strain is another common trigger. But crucially, none of these sources establish a direct causal link between “chest pain when anxious” as an isolated symptom and clinical depression. The presence of physical anxiety manifestations doesn’t confirm or rule out mood disorders on its own.

The right next step isn’t self-diagnosis—it’s getting medically cleared first (any new chest pain warrants ruling out cardiac causes regardless of context), then discussing with a mental health professional if the pattern persists. A clinician would look at duration, severity, functional impairment, and whether you meet full diagnostic criteria for either condition rather than treating this single reportable event as proof of one diagnosis over another.

Refusing to move until you get your deposit back can create serious new problems—even if you have a valid claim to the money itself. Holding over (staying past lease end) typically converts you from tenant to trespasser or holds-over tenant under different rules, which means you might owe rent at higher rates and lose leverage on other issues like habitability claims. In many places, landlords can evict immediately once possession is surrendered late, even with outstanding deposits owed.

The specific answer depends entirely on where you are—California has very different rules than Texas, New York, or London. Some jurisdictions allow tenants to withhold security deposits as "self-help" remedies; others treat any refusal to vacate as an immediate breach that forfeits your rights regardless of what happened before the move-out date. Without knowing your location, I cannot say whether this strategy would work for you specifically.

If you're considering holding over:
- Check if there's a formal holdover clause in your lease (many commercial leases have these)
- Understand that courts often view deposit disputes and possession separately—you might win the money but lose control of when you leave
- Consider whether partial payment plus documentation is safer than full non-compliance with the move-out timeline
